extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of drama/literary theory; playwrights studying Aristotle's Poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and analysing tragic drama (plot, character, diction, thought, music, and spectacle) according to Aristotle's Poetics and accompanying scholarly commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetened language
rubrics_metrics.description: By “sweetened language’ I mean that which has Rhythm, mixture with the unfamiliar, and Tune; by “in different parts in all known ways” that only certain parts are restrained by metres and others again by tune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language may be ‘sweetened’ (1) by limitation/periodical recurrence (rhythm and period); (2) by mixture of the familiar with the foreign (termed 'harmony'); (3) by tune (music—though tune properly belongs to music/politics). These devices tickle the ear and take the hearer out of the real world, making him conscious of the illusion. Only certain parts of the text are so restrained; metre controls syllabic units, tune the semitone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy must include presentation, musical composition, and language (the 'clothing' of the fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the dramatis personae go through their parts themselves, one factor of a Tragedy must necessarily be presentation, another musical composition, and a third language; for these are the clothing of the fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three are the external means by which the fictitious chapter of life is clothed: language (material of versification), musical composition (a thing whose whole force is on the surface), and presentation (the actual staging). Each has a different function and mode of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Factors of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A Tragedy must thus have six Factors, analytically speaking: Story, Psychology (Character), Diction, Intelligence (Thought), Presentation, Music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These six constitute the whole of Tragedy: three (Story/Character/Intelligence) to the Theme, two (Diction/Music) to the Clothing, and one (Presentation) to the Treatment. They are not uniform across all dramatis personae; nearly every character has corresponding externals (story, diction, melody, intellect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Story (Plot) — the primary and most important factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The fictitious chapter of Life is the Story; Tragedy portrays an experience, a condition of life, i.e. a career (an end), and the most important of the six is the group of occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is the 'heart and soul' of tragedy — it portrays an experience and must be a complete, ordered whole. Beginners master diction and psychology sooner than plot-construction. Events (what happens) constitute the ultimate factor to which others must be subordinate; a tragedy could not exist without a career (plot), though it might with scant character depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (Psychology / Ethos)
rubrics_metrics.description: By Character [or Psychology] I mean the traits in virtue of which the fictitious personages have qualities ascribed to them; character is exhibited in both speech and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters derive their qualities from conduct and intellect. The dramatist must give personages characters because the species of a 'farer' (one who fares) is determined by character. Character varies with looks, dress, age, and affects diction and music. Some plays may be unpsychological, but some minimal character must exist; the priority of plot over detailed psychology is emphasised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence (Thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence is the faculty of telling what is within and suits a case; in drama it belongs to passages where characters verbally demonstrate propositions or formulate opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought covers speeches where characters prove, disprove or generalize — matters akin to rhetorical or ethical understanding. It is third in order of importance after plot and character; it belongs especially where the intellectual content of utterance matters rather than mere expression of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (Language / Nomenclature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth of the coefficients is the Diction, meaning Interpretation by nomenclature, which is as effective in verse as in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction is the material of versification and the choice of words/phrases that convey meaning. It is more directly under the poet’s control than presentation; style must suit the characters and the genre (e.g., a child's language plainer than a higher-class personage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Music (Musical composition as a sweetening)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the remainder, Music is the greatest of the sweetenings; a thing whose whole force is on the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music has direct, surface appeal and is 'universal' in some respects — it can be immediately apprehended and does not admit of the multiple interpretability of verbal poetry. The choice of musical modes/harmonies should vary with character and mood; historically some harmonies were used for stage-music because they were imitative/practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation / Spectacle (Exhibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation, though fascinating, is least amenable to scientific treatment, and least connected with Poetry; as a function of Tragedy it does not imply a stage to be divined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle depends largely on actors, costume, and local/historical dressing and is less under the poet’s scientific control. It contributes to effect but is considered a negligible factor for the poet’s art compared with plot and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot completeness and unity (beginning, middle, end; whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy portrays a complete whole, a chapter of life, of some magnitude; that magnitude is a whole which has beginning, middle and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Beginning is that which follows nothing by law of nature but leads to something; an End follows something and is followed by nothing; a Middle both follows and precedes. A well-constructed story must neither begin nor end at a fortuitous point but embody these relations. The whole must be so arranged that removal of any component shatters the whole; no member of the whole should be detachable without loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude and limitation of the plot (quantitative compass)
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful in stories must have some length, but not more than the memory can retain; an adequate quantitative compass is such a quantity of natural or normal sequences as gives room for good fortune to turn into bad fortune or bad fortune into good fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Size should permit the mental synthesis of the spectator; parts must be large enough to show symmetry and arrangement but not so large as to blur the whole. The duration of performance cannot be fixed by science, but the plot must be limited so the audience can grasp the unity; historically some suggested about three hours as practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot should portray a single complete experience (typical episode rather than whole life)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story, as the portrayal of an imaginary experience, should portray one experience and the whole of it; the component parts must be so arranged that displacement of any should disconcert the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet should not attempt to chronicle all events of a life but select a single coherent episode (a 'chapter of life') whose parts cohere by law of nature or moral certainty. The plot is the portrayal of the Potential (what would typically occur), not the chronicling of particular facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should treat the typical/potential (general principles) rather than mere particulars (history)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the poet’s business to treat the actual, but the typical, i.e. the Potential as regulated by moral certainty or laws of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiction generalizes to show what sort of utterances or experiences go with qualities; history particularizes facts. The poet may invent while retaining the most important traditional features; poetry is more 'scientific' in that it formulates general causes/principles rather than only recording particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence of elements with character (consistency across dress, diction, music)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since you have on the stage a king, a princess, a slave, the dress of each, the story of each, the diction of each, and the music corresponding with the character of each will be different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiognomy, age, class and mood dictate looks, dress, language and musical modes. The poet should ensure that diction, melody and presentation fit the character; e.g., child's language must be plainer than a higher-class personage, music varies with mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of psychology (ethos) vs intelligence (thought) in speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychology in the sense of an index to the quality of the purpose has for its sphere places where the ulterior purpose of an immediate resolve is naturally obscure; Intelligence has for its sphere passages where the characters prove, disprove, or generalize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speeches that aim to reveal motive or hidden purpose (where ulterior purpose is not clear) should employ ethos/psychology; speeches that set out arguments, demonstrations, or intellectual propositions belong to Thought/Intelligence. The older dramatists made characters speak naturally (without rhetorical training); modern dramatists often have rhetorically trained speech.
